1	# AGENTS.md
2	
3	Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
4	(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
5	file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.
6	
7	## Project
8	
9	Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
10	built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
11	`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.
12	
13	Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
14	translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
15	instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
16	`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).
17	
18	Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits outside that
19	mechanism — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h`
20	stays self-contained for `osx.c`, which cannot include `sst.h`. Put new
21	display flags there, not in `sst.h`.
22	
23	`osx.c` is the file that cannot include `sst.h`: `sst.h` declares
24	`pause(int)`, which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` that `osx.c`
25	needs. So what `osx.c` *provides* is declared in `osx.h` (included by
26	both `osx.c` and `sst.h`), and what `osx.c` *calls* it gets from
27	`tui.h`. Put new platform functions in `osx.h`, not `sst.h`, so the
28	definition stays checked against the declaration — `-Wmissing-prototypes`
29	is on and CI builds with `-Werror`.
30	
31	## Build and run
32	
33	```sh
34	cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
35	cmake --build build
36	./build/sst
37	```
38	
39	Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
40	without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. `-Wall -Wextra` is always on; CI
41	also configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, so pass that locally to see what
42	CI will refuse. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
43	-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.
44	
45	## TUI mode (`sst -t`)
46	
47	- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
48	  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
49	  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
50	- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
51	  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
52	  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
53	  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
54	  and explain why.
55	- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
56	  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
57	  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
58	  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
59	  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
60	  filter that shape before checking.
61	- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
62	  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
63	  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
64	  sync (`ctest --test-dir build -R tuifmt`).
65	- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
66	  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null
67	  -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 30'`, drive
68	  with `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
69	  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `capture-pane -t t -p`, and clean
70	  up with `kill-server` on that same socket. Without `-f /dev/null` a setting
71	  as ordinary as `base-index 1` renames the pane out from under you and every
72	  capture comes back empty. The default socket is where the
73	  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
74	  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
75	  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
76	  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
77	  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
78	  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
79	  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
80	  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
81	  set.
82	- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
83	  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
84	  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
85	  live.
86	
87	## The golden recordings
88	
89	A failing `golden` test means a journey's output changed. Work out why
90	and say so in the commit -- the fixture diff is the evidence a reviewer
91	needs. Never re-record with `tests/golden.sh <sst> --update` to turn CI
92	green without that explanation; the recordings are the only thing in
93	the suite that checks the game's arithmetic at all.
94	
95	## Development workflow
96	
97	Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.
98	
99	1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
100	   state, all applicable instruction files, and the issue or roadmap item the
101	   work comes from, before making changes. Preserve unrelated staged,
102	   unstaged, and untracked work.
103	
104	2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
105	   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
106	   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
107	   `main` state.
108	
109	3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
110	   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
111	   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
112	   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.
113	
114	   The slice inherits whatever the issue assumes, so check what it claims
115	   before building on it. A claim you can settle — what the code does, what
116	   `sst.doc` says at a given line — you settle, and where it does not hold
117	   you say so on the issue in a comment: what it claimed, what is actually
118	   the case, and the line that shows it. Comment, do not rewrite the issue
119	   body; a comment keeps straight who said what. A closed issue still
120	   takes one, and an issue closed by the pull request that got the premise
121	   wrong is exactly where the correction belongs. Where you cannot comment
122	   at all — a locked issue, a harness with no access to the tracker — say
123	   it in the pull request body and the summary of the work, marked as
124	   unposted.
125	
126	   What is worth building stays the issue author's judgment. A wrong premise
127	   voids the claim it supports, not the issue, and the acceptance criteria
128	   it never touched still bind. Where the facts change what the issue
129	   ought to ask for, say so and ask — do not swap in a slice of your own.
130	   Say what was wrong and what the correction changed about the slice, in
131	   the pull request body and in the summary of the work, in the summary
132	   alone when there is no pull request. Silence is worse than either:
133	   building on a mistake you have seen, or building something else and
134	   leaving the issue describing work nobody did.
135	
136	   #58 is the example, and it reasoned well from one wrong fact. On its
137	   main ground it ruled out checking the galaxy's digit packing because
138	   that packing "appears nowhere in `sst.doc`" — where the manual gives it
139	   at `sst.doc:436-439`, as the meaning of the long-range scan. The
140	   instinct was the one step 4 now endorses, to take an expectation from
141	   somewhere independent of the code; only the fact about where that
142	   source was silent was wrong. It cost a narrower slice than the facts
143	   allowed, not the wrong one.
144

`AGENTS.md:40-42` says CI configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON` and tells the
reader to "pass that locally to see what CI will refuse". The `verifier` is
the pass that stands between a local change and CI, and its definition never
mentions the flag:

```
.claude/agents/verifier.md:19  cmake -S . -B build-debug   -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   && cmake --build build-debug
.claude/agents/verifier.md:20  cmake -S . -B build-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build-release
```

## Why it matters

A warning that CI will reject is invisible to every pass the workflow runs
before CI. The `verifier` reports "zero warnings" from a build that was never
asked to treat them as errors, which reads as the stronger claim.

The gap got sharper with the `### Who runs which tests` section added in
PR #125: that section assigns `-DSST_WERROR=ON` to the `verifier` as one of
"the configurations the main agent did not build". So AGENTS.md now says the
verifier owns it, and `verifier.md` still does not ask for it — on the letter
of the two files, nobody builds it. In practice the sub-agent has been passing
it anyway when told to, which is worse than either: the behaviour depends on
what the invoking prompt happens to say.

## How to see it

Compare `.claude/agents/verifier.md:19-20` against `AGENTS.md:40-42`. Then note
that `AGENTS.md`'s "The review sub-agents" section says a per-tool definition
"should say to read the matching file and follow it, and carry only the wiring
its own harness needs" — the configure lines in `verifier.md` are neither
wiring nor a pointer, they are a restatement that has drifted.

## Fix sketch

Either add `-DSST_WERROR=ON` to both configure lines, or drop the lines and
point at `AGENTS.md`'s "Build and run" section, which already carries the flag
and the reason. The second is what "The review sub-agents" argues for and
cannot drift again.

## Provenance

Found by the `verifier` while verifying PR #125. Filed rather than fixed
there: `verifier.md` is a reviewer definition, and AGENTS.md requires those to
land as their own change, on their own branch and commit, before the work they
review.
EOF

## Verdict

**Fail** — every check I ran is green, but the rewritten paragraph contains a claim that is measurably false, and the classification rule it turns on has a measured counter-example. To answer your closing question plainly: **this is not a further imprecision in prose. It is false, by a factor of eight, about the exact case it was rewritten to classify, and a reader applying the stated criterion literally reaches the opposite conclusion from the one intended.**

## Scope I chose, and why

Note first: I am a fresh session and cannot confirm the two earlier passes — I verified the current worktree from disk. The `AGENTS.md` reaching me through `CLAUDE.md`'s import was the pre-branch version; everything below is read from `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh` on disk.

I did **more** than the count-plus-read you expected, deliberately. The third rewrite converted two judgments into checkable quantitative claims ("take seconds", "under a second") and a discriminating rule about what a mutation must *reach*. Prior rounds' evidence does not cover assertions that did not exist then, so I measured all three rather than reading them. I did **not** re-run the full `ctest` battery, Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, or the TUI journeys: nothing executable changed, and the one executable file in the branch diff I re-ran in three shells anyway.

## Findings

### 1. The tree-vs-binary rewrite is false in both halves (deterministic, measured)

> "A mutation that has to reach the compiled binary brings a copied tree and a journey with it, and is worth a sub-agent; one that only has to reach a file the game reads as data, or a test that reads the tree without running the game, is proved from a few copied files in under a second"

**(a) The data-file half, on the `help.sh` case that motivated it.** I copied exactly two files (`sst.doc`, `tests/help.sh`) to `/tmp/helpmut`, mutated `Full command:` → `Fyll cimmand:` in the copied `sst.doc`, and ran the *repo's existing* `build-debug/sst` against it — no rebuild, as the wording predicts.

```
sh /tmp/helpmut/tests/help.sh .../build-debug/sst
FAIL: help printed no documentation (expected output to contain: Full command:)
```

The mutation is correctly reachable with no rebuild — that part of your analysis holds. But the timing does not: **8.33s, 8.22s, 8.22s across three runs** (deterministic, not flaky), against a clean `tests/help.sh` baseline of 8.31s. `help.sh` plays the whole game three times, and on failure it dumps 2048 bytes of screen — which is precisely "the run and the output it dumps" that the sentence two lines above names as *the* cost. The paragraph's own cost model contradicts its classification of its own example.

**(b) The compiled-binary half.** Counter-example measured: mutate `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tuifmt.c:24`, `condit != IHDOCKED` → `condit == IHDOCKED` (the sensor-damage mask; `test_tuifmt` links only `tuifmt.c`, so its expectations are literals in its own file — an independent break, not shared descent). In a copied tree: configure+build 1.68s, `ctest -R tuifmt` 0.04s, **1.72s total**, test fails. It brings a copied tree but **no journey**, and it is not worth a sub-agent — the section's own line 343 already says a `ctest -R` costs a second.

**Why the rule misses:** the property that tracks cost is not what the mutation has to reach, it is whether the *test* runs the whole game and how many times. Both counter-examples fall straight out of that: a data mutation with three game runs costs 8.2s; a binary mutation with no game run costs 1.7s. `help.sh` is the near-miss for the *reachability* framing too — it just misses in the other direction from the one the wording assumes.

**Why it is actionable, not cosmetic:** a reader who applies "under a second" as the stated threshold measures `help.sh` at 8 seconds with a 2 KB dump, sees it fail the criterion as written, and delegates it — the opposite of what the paragraph is for. The conclusion you want (do it yourself; 8s beats a sub-agent round trip) is right; the reason given does not support it and the criterion as written points away from it.

### 2. Cost attribution rewrite — true as written

> "the configure and build, which take seconds"

Measured fresh: rsync copy 0.15s, configure 1.05s, build `-j24` 0.60s (**1.79s total**); serial configure+build **4.36s**. `tests/golden.sh` run: **43.41s** (exit 0, `golden OK`). The attribution is correct for the whole-game tests it is about. Minor, not a finding: for the compiled unit tests the ordering inverts (build 1.68s vs run 0.04s), but everything there is seconds, so nothing turns on it.

### 3. Shape/cost rewrite — true and consistent

"Shape decides whether it may be… Cost decides whether it is worth it" is coherent with the rest of the section and with step 4. The `tui.sh` line ("belongs in the loop, slow as it is") is exactly a shape-first case — shape rules out delegation and cost never gets a vote — so the displacement problem you were fixing is gone. No conflict found with step 4's inserted "Run that loop yourself rather than delegating it."

### 4. Secondary: step 4's mutation-proof bullets carry no pointer to the refinement

`AGENTS.md:167-178` prescribes copying the working tree and configuring a fresh build, scoped by `AGENTS.md:165-166` to "tests that run the whole game and read what it printed" — which `help.sh` is. # Verdict: FAIL

Four measurable problems, one of them introduced by this round's edit. Everything executable is green; nothing I ran flaked (repeated runs listed at the end).

---

## Failures

### 1. The mutation proof recorded in `tests/instructions.sh` no longer reproduces — this round broke it — **false**

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh:211-218` says:

> `Mutate with something that spans newlines, and take both: either alone leaves the check satisfied, which is the check working as designed and not a mutation that failed to apply.`

There are now **three** quoted pointers, not two. This round added one at `AGENTS.md:189-191` (the new step 4 bullet), on top of `AGENTS.md:152-154` (step 4's loop pointer) and `AGENTS.md:231-232` (step 7's).

Measured against the current `AGENTS.md`, in a temp copy:

```
# removed exactly the two pointers the comment names (step 4 loop + step 7)
$ sh tests/instructions.sh /tmp/instr-mut.XXXX
instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 27705 bytes)   exit=0
# then removed the third (the new bullet) as well
FAIL: nothing in AGENTS.md points forward at "Who runs which tests" ...   exit=1
```

Deterministic. So a reader following the comment literally gets a green run and, on the comment's own advice, concludes the mutation failed to apply — which is exactly the failure mode the paragraph was written to prevent. "Removing only step 4's still passes" is also now ambiguous: step 4 holds two pointers.

The check itself is not blind — heading rename → FAIL, all three pointers gone → FAIL, both verified above. It is the recorded procedure that is stale.

### 2. "Pipe the shell tests through `tail`" — **false, and a reader could act on it wrongly**

`AGENTS.md:363-365`. Two measurements against it:

- On a pass, every test in this suite prints **exactly one line** (extracted from `build-verify-debug/Testing/Temporary/LastTest.log`): `tuifmt` 17 B, `rules` 17 B, `journey` 24 B, `journey-tui` 24 B, `eof` 7 B, `help` 8 B, `tui` 7 B, `tournament` 32 B, `golden` 10 B, `instructions` 61 B, `score` 31 B. I confirmed fresh: `sh tests/tui.sh ./build-debug/sst` → `tui OK`, 1 line, 7 bytes. There is nothing for `tail` to trim, so "written for a human watching them run" does not describe them.
- On a failure `tail` is the wrong filter. With `sst.c`'s CR-strip mutated in a copied tree, `tests/help.sh` produced 62 lines / 2154 bytes, and `FAIL: help output still carries sst.doc's carriage returns` is **line 1**. `2>&1 | tail -n 20` shows 20 lines of manual text plus `1 check(s) failed.` and drops the only line saying what broke. Without `2>&1`, `tail` sees an empty stdout and filters nothing — the FAIL text and the whole dump reach the terminal anyway.

### 3. "A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the golden recordings regression surface" — **false**

`AGENTS.md:338-340`. Measured: in a copied tree with `tuifmt.c:24` mutated to `return 0; /* MUTATION: sensor masking disabled */`, `sh tests/golden.sh <copy>/build/sst` printed `golden OK` in 43.4s. `tests/golden.sh:101` runs the binary plainly — no `-t` anywhere in it — and the panel formatters (`fmt_quad_line`, `fmt_status_line`, `cell_class`, `status_class`, `sensors_masked`) are called only from `tui.c`. The one function in that file reachable from plain mode is `condition_now()` (`setup.c:577`), so the recordings are not entirely blind to the file, but they are blind to what the file is about and what `AGENTS.md:61-64` says it must mirror. The real regression surface for a `tuifmt.c` change is `tui` / `journey-tui`.

### 4. "neither the copy nor the build behind it is where the cost turns out to be" — **false for the paragraph's own cheap example**

`AGENTS.md:381-383`, and the sentence immediately before it says `Time it`. Timed, on the `tuifmt.c` case in a fresh copy:

| phase | time | output |
|---|---|---|
| rsync copy (39 MB, no `build*`/`.git`) | 0.16 s | 0 lines |
| `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` | 1.06 s | 17 lines |
| `cmake --build build --target test_tuifmt` | 0.46 s | 4 lines |
| `ctest --test-dir build -R tuifmt --output-on-failure` (pass) | 0.026 s | 7 lines / 220 B |
| rebuild after mutating `tuifmt.c` | 0.36 s | 3 lines |
| same `ctest` (fail) | 0.033 s | 34 lines / 922 B |

Copy + configure + build = 2.04 s of a 2.07 s total, ~97% of the elapsed cost; the two `ctest` runs are 0.06 s of it. For the `help.sh` case (full `cmake --build`, 3.25 s) it is 4.5 s of 21.4 s, 21%. So on the quantity the adjacent sentence tells the reader to measure, the claim is inverted for one of the two cases and holds for the other.

Charitable reading, which you may prefer to argue: "the cost" means "what makes a proof expensive enough to delegate", and by that reading nothing here is expensive — 2 s and 21 s. If that is the intent, the sentence as written still points a reader at the wrong measurement.

Related, same paragraph: `Time it` measures seconds, but the stated criterion is context volume. Timing `help.sh` yields 8.2 s (21 s for the whole proof) and says nothing about the 62 lines it dumps.

---

So the slowest single test is `tui` at 55-106 s — under two minutes against the 4-18 minute round trips you observed. The claim is true for a single test.

One wrinkle, **prose imprecision**: those same figures sum to 252.8 s Debug / 243.5 s Release / 209.9 / 200.4 s, which is the "about four minutes per configuration" of `AGENTS.md:355-356` — inside your round-trip range. 2	# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
3	# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
4	#
5	# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
6	# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
7	# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
8	# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
9	# truth that slowly disagree.
10	#
11	# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
12	# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
13	# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
14	# an agent session with no rules at all.
15	#
16	# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root
17	
18	set -u
19	
20	ROOT="${1:-.}"
21	while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
22		ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
23	done
24	CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
25	AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"
26	
27	# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
28	# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
29	# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
30	# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
31	# that one is left to review.
32	MAXBYTES=220
33	# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
34	# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
35	# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
36	# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
37	# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
38	# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
39	MAXLINES=4
40	# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
41	MINAGENTS=2000
42	
43	fails=0
44	fail() {
45		printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
46		fails=$((fails + 1))
47	}
48	
49	if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
50		fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
51	fi
52	if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
53		fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
54	fi
55	if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
56		exit 1
57	fi
58	
59	agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
60	claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')
61	
62	# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
63	if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
64		fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
65	fi
66	if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
67		fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
68	fi
69	
70	# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
71	# in one form of words so a reader can see that they agree. They did not
72	# always: two said "address every actionable finding" and the middle one
73	# said "fix or explicitly resolve", while the first claimed to be
74	# stating the same rule "as with the two steps below". Nobody noticed
75	# until a reviewer read all three together.
76	#
77	# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
78	# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
79	# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
80	# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
81	# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is where
82	# that check would live -- as filed it checks numbering, not which step
83	# a match fell in; the comment thread there asks for the attribution it
84	# would need.
85	#
86	# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
87	# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
88	# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
89	# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
90	# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
91	# quietly turn this into something else.
92	STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
93	# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
94	# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
95	STANDARDS=4
96	# Awk's status and its output are both checked, because either can lie
97	# on its own. A non-number means it did not run -- unsupported construct,
98	# missing binary, anything -- and compared directly against STANDARDS
99	# that is a silent pass rather than a failure: the test errors "Illegal
100	# number", `if` reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes
101	# on to print "instructions OK". A number from a command that then
102	# failed is the same hole from the other side: a shadowed awk printing
103	# "4" and exiting 17 satisfied the number check, and did it on a file
104	# whose step 8 had been reworded back to the old standard -- green,
105	# with the defect present and the counter never having run.
106	if ! standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
107		{ s = s " " $0 }
108		END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS"); then
109		fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run whatever it printed"
110	else
111		case "$standards" in
112		'' | *[!0-9]*)
113			fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
114			;;
115		*)
116			if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
117				fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
118			fi
119			;;
120		esac
121	fi
122	# AGENTS.md keeps some of its rules in named sections below the numbered
123	# steps, with the steps pointing forward at them by name. Both halves have
124	# to hold: a heading nothing points at is unreachable, and a pointer with
125	# no heading sends a reader nowhere. Checked for each such section by
126	# name, so adding one means adding a call rather than a second copy of
127	# this.
128	#
129	# $1 heading text, $2 what is lost if the heading goes, $3 what is lost if
130	# the pointer goes.
131	#
132	# Prefix-matched, so a heading renamed to "### Answering a finding here"
133	# satisfies this while every pointer names a heading that is gone. That
134	# is issue #105, and the pointer check matches the same way: awk's
135	# index() is literal rather than a BRE, which is a different property,
136	# but it is still a substring search and a longer heading satisfies it
137	# too. Fixing one without the other fixes nothing.
138	check_section() {
139		if ! grep -q "^### $1" "$AGENTS"; then
140			# Returning here rather than going on to the pointer: with no
141			# heading that check reports that nothing points forward, which
142			# is true but reads as a second, separate defect when the
143			# pointer is sitting there untouched.
144			fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $1' section -- $2"
145			return
146		fi
147		# The pointer is the one thing tying the numbered steps to the
148		# section. Delete just that clause and the heading is still there:
149		# the section goes on existing with nothing sending a reader to it.
150		# For "Answering a finding" that loses the half of #97 that asked
151		# where a disagreement is recorded, and the standard count above
152		# still reads 4 while it happens. Matched in quotes because the
153		# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not
154		# the thing referred to.
155		#
156		# Before the heading, specifically. A mention below it is a
157		# back-reference and cannot send anyone anywhere: the reader is
158		# already there. Counting mentions instead would pass on a file
159		# where the step's pointer was deleted and the section itself quoted
160		# its own name -- one mention either way -- which is the state this

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i3.md" <<'EOF'
`CMakeLists.txt:107-108`, on the `tournament` test:

> About 50 seconds here, the slowest test in the suite by four times --
> nearly all of it the busy-wait that types the game's dramatic lines
> out slowly.

Three claims, and the arithmetic is wrong in all three. Measured from
`CTestCostData.txt` left behind by full-battery runs on this machine:

| | `build-verify-debug` | `build-ci-debug` |
|---|---|---|
| `tui` | 105.6 s | 63.6 s |
| `tournament` | 69.5 s | 69.0 s |
| `golden` | 44.1 s | 43.3 s |
| `eof` | 19.4 s | 19.2 s |

- **"About 50 seconds"** — it is about 69, consistently, across every run
  recorded here.
- **"the slowest test in the suite"** — not reliably. `tui` beat it by 36
  seconds on one run and lost by 5 on another, so which is slowest depends on
  the machine and on whether tmux is present at all.
- **"by four times"** — the next test down is `golden` at 43 s. The margin is
  about 1.6x on the run where `tournament` leads, and negative on the other.

## Why it matters

The comment is the only place in the tree that says what the suite costs, and
it is what a reader consults before deciding whether to run something. It
understates `tournament` by a third and points at the wrong test entirely,
which is exactly backwards for anyone budgeting a run — `tui` is the one that
can take a minute and three quarters.

It also now disagrees with `AGENTS.md`'s "Who runs which tests" section, which
tells a reader that no single test runs longer than two minutes and names the
tests whose failure output is worth avoiding.

## How to see it

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build
sort -k3 -rn build/Testing/Temporary/CTestCostData.txt | head -5
```

## Fix sketch

Replace the three figures with what the file can actually stand behind, or
drop the comparison and keep only the shape of the cost — that nearly all of
it is the busy-wait typing the dramatic lines, which is the part that explains
the `TIMEOUT 300` sitting under it and is still true. A number in a comment
that nothing measures goes stale the first time a test is added; this one is
already two claims past that.

## Provenance

Found by the `verifier` while verifying the `docs/agents-test-split` branch,
which added a section about test cost and prompted the measurement. Filed
rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9 — it is a comment the change did
not touch.

content.text:
# Verdict: **fail**

Three claims in the diff are false or unsafe as written. The four fixes you asked about are, individually, in better shape than last round — findings 1, 2 and 3 all reproduce exactly, and the STANDARDS count is right. Finding 4 is where it went wrong: two of its numbers do not survive measurement, and one of its recommendations, applied to the test the same paragraph singles out, leaks a live tmux server.

---

## Failures (false / actionable — fix)

### F1. "No single test here longer than two minutes" is false for the runs the paragraph is about
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:379-381`

> No single test here runs longer than two minutes, against sub-agent round trips of several, so nothing is finished sooner by delegating it.

The paragraph's subject is the mutation proof — a run you expect to **fail**. A failing `tui.sh` exceeds two minutes. Measured against `/tmp/brk1` (working tree copied out, `fmt_status_line`'s `"Stardate      %.1f"` → `"Sardate       %.1f"`, fresh Debug build there):

```
cd /tmp/brk1 && time sh tests/tui.sh /tmp/brk1/build/sst
  run 1: real 2m4.098s   3 failed assertions
  run 2: real 2m3.638s   3 failed assertions
```

**Deterministic**, not flaky — two runs, 0.5 s apart, both over the bound, with only *three* failures. Passing runs are comfortably under it (96.5 s, 96.6 s, 105.4 s), so the claim is true only for the case the paragraph is not about. The polling helpers are what does it: failures routed through `expect`/`wait_gone_status` wait out their full timeout, where failures through `want` return at once (banner break, 3 failures: 96.8 s; panel-title break, 19 failures: 105.9 s).

The repository already says so: `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakeLists.txt:95-101` sets `TIMEOUT 300` on `tui` with the comment "a broadly broken TUI spends its time timing out one poll at a time. Better that it reaches the end and names each failure than that ctest kills it". That is the project's own estimate of a failing run's cost, and it is 2.5x the figure in the diff.

### F2. "some thirty of them" is off by a factor of four
`AGENTS.md:383-385`

> `tui.sh` prints a whole pane per failed assertion and has some thirty of them

`tests/tui.sh` has **133** assertion sites that dump a pane: 42 call sites of the ten helpers that dump (`want`, `expect`, `expect_re`, `expect_status`, `want_quadtitle`, `wait_gone_status`, `unwanted`, `wait_gone`, `replay_case`, `fallback`) plus 91 inline `dump`/`dump_scrollback` invocations in test bodies. Thirty is not a count of anything in the file — sections are 22 (`^# --- `), `start` calls 24, `fail` call sites 106.

One realistic break (panel titles `" Status "`/`" Quadrant "` mangled in `tui.c`) produced **19 dumps, 456 lines, 21036 bytes**. The conclusion the paragraph draws survives — 21 KB does bury a context — but the number offered as the basis for it does not.

The "whole pane per failed assertion" half is exact: `tests/tui.sh:145-148` is `dump() { printf '  --- screen ---\n'; screen | sed 's/^/  | /'; }` over `capture-pane -t "$pane" -p`, measured at ~26 lines / ~1.4 KB per dump at 24-row sizes.

### F3. The recommended `2>&1 | head` kills `tests/tui.sh` mid-run and leaks a tmux server
`AGENTS.md:365-369`

Run verbatim, with the doc's bare `head`:

```
cd /tmp/brk2 && sh tests/tui.sh /tmp/brk2/build/sst 2>&1 | head
```

`head` exits after 10 lines, `tui.sh` takes SIGPIPE, and its `EXIT` trap never runs. Left behind, measured:

```
3192071 tmux -f /dev/null -L sst-tui-3192013 new-session -d -x 72 -y 24 -s tui -c /tmp/brk2 '/tmp/brk2/build/sst' -t ; sleep 30
3192077 /tmp/brk2/build/sst -t
/tmp/tmux-1000/sst-tui-3192013          (socket file)
/tmp/sst-tui.BvUTcs                     (temp dir)
```

**Deterministic** — reproduced with `head -3` and again with bare `head`. A single pane dump is ~26 lines, so the 10-line default is always exceeded by the first failure.

Mechanism confirmed in isolation (`/tmp/pipetest.sh`): a script with `tui.sh`'s exact trap set loses its `EXIT` trap on SIGPIPE; adding `trap 'finish; exit 141' PIPE` restores it. `tests/tui.sh:91-94` is the only one of the four dumping shell tests without that PIPE trap — `tests/help.sh:42`, `tests/tournament.sh:103` and `tests/golden.sh:73` all have it.

Pipe it into anything that can exit early — `head`, `grep -q`, `less` and a
`q` — and the script takes SIGPIPE, dies, and its `EXIT` trap never runs.
`finish` is what kills the private tmux server, so what is left behind is:

- a `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst-tui-<pid>` server, still running
- the `sst -t` process inside it, still running
- the socket under `/tmp/tmux-1000/`
- the `/tmp/sst-tui.XXXXXX` working directory

Reproduced by the `verifier` with both `head -3` and a bare `head`. A single
pane dump is about 26 lines, so `head`'s 10-line default is exceeded by the
first failing assertion — this needs no unusual invocation, only a failing run
that someone pipes.

## It has already happened

Two orphans are sitting on this machine right now, from before the branch that
found this:

```
/tmp/sst-tui.474IVX   Aug 10 19:27
/tmp/sst-tui.6Q7RWJ   Aug  8 20:43
```

with matching tmux servers still alive. Nobody noticed, which is the point:
the leak is silent, and the server has a per-run name nobody would think to
look for.

## Why it matters beyond the litter

`AGENTS.md` tells every agent to keep test output out of its context, and the
obvious way to do that is a pipe. So the advice most likely to be followed is
the one that trips this. The `### Who runs which tests` section added on
`docs/agents-test-split` now has to tell readers to redirect to a file rather
than pipe, and cite this issue for why — which is a workaround in an
instruction file standing in for a one-line fix in a test.

## Fix sketch

```sh
trap 'finish; exit 141' PIPE
```

matching the other three scripts. Worth checking at the same time whether
`finish` is safe to run when a write to stdout is what failed — it calls
`tmux kill-server` on its own socket, which does not write to stdout, so it
should be.

The `verifier` also noted the general shape: nothing checks that these four
scripts agree on their trap sets. That is a second, smaller issue if anyone
wants it.

## Provenance

Found by the `verifier` while verifying the `docs/agents-test-split` branch,
when the branch's own advice to pipe test output was measured. Filed rather
than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9 — it is a defect the change did not
cause. The two orphaned servers above were left alone; they are not this
session's, and `AGENTS.md` forbids a bare `tmux kill-server`.

### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs everything else.** The line does not fall between unit
tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about. A change to the
pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs in the loop, slow
as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled `tuifmt` test the
focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest to the `verifier`
— including
the golden recordings, which never pass `-t` and so cannot see that file's
panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach.

Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all. It asks you to watch a test fail
for the expected reason, and a sub-agent reporting that it failed correctly
is exactly the trust that failing run exists to withhold. It is also the
tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes
against a `ctest -R` that costs a second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest --output-on-failure` prints no test output on a pass, and `-R`
  scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern, since it is a
  regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On
  a failure they print what broke and then dump the screen behind it, in
  that order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the
  last. Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop it
belongs to. Shape decides whether it may be: the loop is iterative and each
failure decides the next edit, which is why you watch it yourself, where the
proof is one shot, asked and answered.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here comes near a
sub-agent round trip even when it fails, and a failing run is what a proof is:

instead, which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than

## Verdict: pass

All three fixes (F1-F3) hold, and the three prose items (P1-P3) are answered. Three new prose observations below, none of them false claims — they are for the pull request body if you disagree with them.

### Scope I chose

`git diff` shows exactly two modified files, no staged and no untracked content: `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh`. `instructions.sh` has an mtime of `23:20`, before my previous round's own artifacts (`23:30`-`23:48`), which corroborates your "byte-identical" claim independently of your word for it. So I re-ran only the instructions test (direct and through `ctest`), `shellcheck`, one plain-mode smoke journey, and then spent the round on the claims you listed. No builds, no full battery, no `tui.sh` — nothing compiled changed, and re-running the battery over a docs diff buys nothing.

Two of your figures I did *not* have to take on trust: my previous round left its artifacts in `/tmp`, and they are still there. That is where the F1 and F2 confirmations below come from.

### Findings

**F1 — RESOLVED, and now measured rather than argued.** The 2m04s is exact. `/tmp/brk1-tui.out` was created at `23:31:18.520` (the redirect opening = process start) and `/tmp/brk1-tui.err` last written at `23:33:22.602` — 2m04.1s. "Goes past two minutes" is true of that run.

**F2 — RESOLVED, transcribed correctly, and conservatively.** `/tmp/brk4-tui.err`: 19 occurrences of `--- screen`, 19 `FAIL` lines, 456 lines total. Subtracting the 19 headers and 19 fail lines leaves 418 lines of pane. "Nineteen panes and four hundred lines of them" is right and rounds down.

**F3 — RESOLVED.** Every part of the citation checks out against the files on disk, not a copy: `tests/help.sh:42`, `tests/golden.sh:73`, `tests/tournament.sh:103` each `trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE`; `tests/tui.sh:91-94` has the four traps and no `PIPE`. Issue #128 is open, titled "tests/tui.sh has no PIPE trap, so a closed pipe leaks a tmux server", and its body matches what AGENTS.md attributes to it. Both orphaned `/tmp/sst-tui.*` directories are still present and untouched.

**`-R` regex claim — CONFIRMED exactly.** `ctest -N -R tui` in `build-debug` returns three tests: `tuifmt` (#1), `journey-tui` (#4), `tui` (#7). `ctest -N -R '^tui$'` returns one. `-R` is a regex, and both halves of the sentence are literally what the tool does.

**P3 — the added clause does close it.** `condition_now()` is defined in `tuifmt.c:27`, declared in `sst.h:456`, and called from `setup.c:577` (`newcnd()`), which every plain-mode game runs — so the goldens genuinely do reach into that file, which is what the old sentence over-generalized away. The narrowed claim is true: `fmt_quad_line`, `fmt_status_line`, `cell_class`, `status_class` and `sensors_masked` have no caller outside `tuifmt.c` and `tui.c`, and every `tui.c` path into them is behind `tui_active` — `tui_gameover()` (`tui.c:714-717`) is the one entry point called unguarded from `finish.c`, `events.c` and `sst.c`, and it tests the flag itself. `tests/golden.sh` never passes `-t` (`play()` at line 101 runs `run "$SST"` with no flags). "Cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach" is now exactly right.

**`STANDARDS` — CONFIRMED at 4.** The script's own awk over the flattened file prints `4`; the matches are at `AGENTS.md:213`, `:227`, `:237`, `:471`. The new section adds no fifth statement of the phrase. `sh tests/instructions.sh .` prints `instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 28688 bytes)`, exit 0; `ctest -R '^instructions$'` passes in 0.05s; `shellcheck -s sh tests/instructions.sh` is clean.

### New prose observations (not failures)

**P4 — the two minutes is not mostly the polls.** From `/tmp/ctest-debug.log`, a *passing* `tui` on this machine takes 105.43s. The broken run took 124s. So the failing run's excess over a passing one is about 19 seconds, and "a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes waiting out its polls" reads as though the polls are what put it past two minutes when a passing run is already at 1m45s. The sentence's load-bearing point — that it stays well under a round trip — is unaffected. Related and outside this diff: `CMakeLists.txt:93` says "the ~11s it takes to pass", which is off by a factor of ten on this machine; that is a candidate for step 9, not for this branch.

**P5 — "even when it fails" is bounded for breaks that change output, not for breaks that hang.** Everything I measured supports it (worst case `tui` at 2m04s; my broken-`tournament` run at `23:44` finished in about a minute). But `tests/tournament.sh` plays 14 seeds each under `timeout 60` (`:110`, `:257`), so a mutation that makes the game hang rather than print something different runs up to 14 minutes standalone, and gets killed at `TIMEOUT 300` under ctest. Low severity: a mutation proof normally changes output. Worth a clause only if you want the sentence airtight.

**P6 — the file does not follow its own new advice one screen earlier.** The first hunk changes the TUI bullet to `ctest --test-dir build -R tuifmt`, unanchored, while the new bullet says to anchor. Nothing checks any measured claim inside the section: the two-minute figure, the nineteen panes, the four-minute `ctest` budget, the `#128` citation, or that the `-R` examples name tests that exist. for the expected reason, and a sub-agent reporting that it failed correctly
is exactly the trust that failing run exists to withhold. It is also the
tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes
against a `ctest -R` that costs a second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of

the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.

commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

content.content:
### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.



Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent
cannot be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run
and the work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the
task, and a report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was
supposed to inform. It is also the tightest loop in the workflow, where a
sub-agent round trip costs minutes against a `ctest -R` that costs a
second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. `verifier.md` does not yet ask for that flag, which is #125; until it
does, say so when invoking the pass. It decides that scope for itself: step
7 gives it the criterion, and step 8 says the decision is the verifier's
own. This says only that it should not be asked to skip what the main agent
happened to run, and that the main agent should not pre-run the battery to
save it the trouble. Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the
whole of it: a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.



**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop it
belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot, asked and
answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name, and step
4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not give it is
visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and this one has to break the game. A general-purpose sub-agent
does it, on a copy outside the repository, which step 4 requires in any
case: no file in the repository is modified.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here comes near a
sub-agent round trip even when it fails, and a failing run is what a proof
is: a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes, its failed polls waiting out
their timeouts on top of a run that is slow already, where a round trip is
several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context instead,
which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than guessing —
one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four hundred lines
of them, `tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails,
`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are
below it — a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in a second, a `help` journey
in eight — running it costs less than handing it over.



When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

### The review sub-agents

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i5.md" <<'EOF'
`check_section()` in `tests/instructions.sh` locates a section heading with:

```sh
grep -q "^### $1" "$AGENTS"
```

`$1` is interpolated into a basic regular expression. The pointer half of the
same function passes `$1` to `awk -v` and searches with `index()`, which is
literal. The comment above the function notes that the two "match the same
way" as a substring search and calls the difference "a different property",
but never says that one side is a regex and the other is not.

## Why it matters

Neither section name has a metacharacter today, so nothing is wrong now:

```
check_section 'Answering a finding' ...
check_section 'Who runs which tests' ...
```

The function is the documented extension point — its own comment says "adding
one means adding a call rather than a second copy of this" — so the next name
is written by someone following that instruction, and nothing warns them. A
heading like `### The 3.x flags` or `### Answering a finding (and when not to)`
matches a different set of lines through `grep` than through `index()`, and the
two halves of the check would then disagree about whether the section exists.
Backslashes are worse: `grep` consumes them and `awk -v` consumes them again.

The failure is silent in the direction that matters — a heading check that
matches too loosely passes, which is the same shape as #105.

## How to see it

```sh
sed -i 's/^### Answering a finding$/### Answering a finding./' AGENTS.md
sh tests/instructions.sh .        # passes: `.` matches the real heading's own text
```

## Fix sketch

Match the heading literally on both sides — `grep -qF -- "### $1"` loses the
line anchor, so either `awk 'index($0, "### " s) == 1'` for both halves, or
keep `grep` and escape the name. Whichever, the two halves should use the same
matching rule, since the comment already claims they do.

Worth doing together with #105 and #126: all three are about this check being
looser than it reads, and a rewrite that gives it per-step attribution would
be the moment to make the matching literal as well.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` while verifying the `docs/agents-test-split` branch,
which generalized the hard-coded check into `check_section()` and so turned a
latent property of one call into an extension point. Filed rather than fixed
there, per AGENTS.md step 9.
EOF

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop in the
step it belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot,
asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,
and step 4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not
give it is visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here costs more
than a sub-agent round trip, even when it fails, and a failing run is what a
proof is: a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes, its failed polls waiting
out their timeouts on top of a run that is slow already, where a round trip
is several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context instead,
which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than guessing —
one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four hundred lines
of them, `tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails,
`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are
below it — a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in a second, a `help` journey
in eight — running it costs less than handing it over.

When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

## Finding 1 — actionable, factual. "seven lines" and "one line" are correct, but they are pass-run counts sitting in a sentence about failing runs

Both numbers you asked about are exactly right as stated:

- `ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$'` on a pass: **7 lines** (ctest 4.2.3, full output including chrome). Confirmed.
- `tests/help.sh <sst>` on a pass: **1 line** (`help OK`). Confirmed — and it is one line for every shell test in the suite, which I checked individually rather than by inference: `eof OK`, `journey OK (3710 bytes)`, `golden OK`, `score OK (27 lines, column 47)`, `instructions OK (...)`, `tournament OK (14 seeds, Debug)`, `tui OK`. Eight for eight, one line each.

The problem is the frame. The sentence before them is "delegate when the failing run would bury this context", and the three examples that follow it are all failing-run volumes — 1209 lines, 3000 bytes per failing seed, a diff per changed journey. "Below that ... a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in seven lines, a `help` journey in one" is parallel construction on a list of failure outputs, so "answering" reads as answering a break. Measured, on the copy at `/tmp/sst-copy`:

| proof | pass | fail |
|---|---|---|
| `ctest -R '^tuifmt$' --output-on-failure`, one assertion broken (`status_class` case 8 returns `STAT_GOOD`) | 7 lines | **16 lines** |
| same, broader break (`sensors_masked()` returns 1) — 7 assertions | 7 lines | **34 lines** |
| `tests/help.sh`, CR strip broken at `sst.c:188` | 1 line | **62 lines / 2154 bytes** |

`help.sh` caps each dump at `DUMPBYTES=2048` and has three `dump_if_failed` blocks, so its ceiling is nearer 6 KB than one line.

This does not falsify the paragraph's conclusion — 16, 34 and 62 are all far below 1209, so "there is nothing to bury, so keep it" survives with room to spare. But it is the same species as the four comparators that came before it: a number that is true of one thing, offered in a position where it reads as a number about another. Either qualify them as pass output, or use the failure figures, which make the argument better rather than worse (62 against 1209 is still an order of magnitude).

## Finding 2 — actionable, factual. `-R '^tuifmt$'` reaches one of the two compiled tests, and the bullet says "the compiled ones"

`rules` is the other one — `add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)` at `CMakeLists.txt:59`, from `tests/test_rules.c` + `rules.c`. `ctest -N -R '^tuifmt$'` returns Total Tests: 1.

The anchoring itself is correct and the finding it answers is fixed: `^tuifmt$` no longer drags in `journey-tui` and `tui` the way bare `tui` does (I confirmed `-R tui` still selects all three, so the warning in "Who runs which tests" is accurate). What is off is the plural. An agent who has just written an assertion in `tests/test_rules.c`, follows the bullet literally, and runs `-R '^tuifmt$'` on the broken copy gets `1/1 Test #1: tuifmt ... Passed` — a green run produced by never having run the test under proof, which is precisely the "the test is blind, or the break was" trap two bullets later, arriving by a third route the bullet itself supplied.

`-R '^(tuifmt|rules)$'` works (`ctest -N` returns both), as does naming `rules` separately. Alternatively, mark `tuifmt` as an example rather than as the set.

## Finding 3 — actionable, factual, pre-existing text inside the sentence the diff edits

The clause the diff amends sits in this sentence, whose opening is unchanged context:

> Every test here takes the binary as an argument, so the run is `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`, or `ctest --test-dir <copy>/build -R '^tuifmt$'` for the compiled ones

"Every test here takes the binary as an argument" is false for two of the eleven registered tests. `instructions` and `score` take the source directory — `CMakeLists.txt:122-124` and `131-133` both pass `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}`, and `sh tests/instructions.sh .` is how you ran the very check under review. The "so" makes it load-bearing: it is the premise from which the two example commands are drawn. Raising it because `code-review` is about to re-read this sentence for the third time and it is now half-new; not because the diff introduced it.

---

## Your question 1: can anything in the new paragraph be false?

I went through it clause by clause.

- **"a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated"** — holds, in the one direction it asserts. A sub-agent invocation blocks the parent, so a delegated 3-minute run costs the parent ≥ 3 minutes plus round-trip. It cannot come out cheaper. The single hinge is that blocking property: if a harness ever offered a genuinely detached sub-agent, "no cheaper" would become false. That is a property of the tool, not of this repository, and today it holds. Stating it as "no cheaper" rather than "more expensive" is what keeps it safe — the narrower claim is the one that survives.
- **"one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()` made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes"** — reproduced exactly, from a fresh copy and a fresh build: `if (1) return;` after the declarations at `tui.c:726`, `tests/tui.sh /tmp/sst-copy/build/sst Debug` → 3m05.3s, **1209 lines, 47 FAILs**, exit 1. Identical to the prior session's numbers; deterministic, not flaky. This is the one number in the paragraph that will drift silently — it is a function of how many checks `tui.sh` currently has and of the 80x24/72x24 pane geometry, so any added TUI check moves it.
- **"`tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails"** — true. `DUMPBYTES=3000` at `tests/tournament.sh:90`, `tail -c "$DUMPBYTES"` at line 663, inside the per-seed loop guarded by `if [ "$fails" -ne "$before" ]`.
- **"`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey"** — true. `tests/golden.sh:154-164`, per journey, `cmp` then `diff | head -n "$DIFFLINES"` with `DIFFLINES=40`.
- **"most proofs are below it"** — not falsifiable, and reads as the judgment it is.

- "`verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is #125" — true; no `SST_WERROR` anywhere in `.claude/agents/`. #125 open, titled to match.
- "all of them are read-only by definition" — true for all three agent files.

## Your question 3 — the `STANDARDS` count and the pointer count

Both right.

- `STANDARDS=4`: the flattened count of `actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly` in the current `AGENTS.md` is **4**. The new section adds no fifth statement of it, so the constant needed no change.
- Pointer count: **3** quoted `"Who runs which tests"` after flattening — `AGENTS.md:152` (step 4, beside the loop), `191` (step 4, beside the mutation-proof bullets), `233` (step 7). The comment in `instructions.sh` describing this is accurate down to the wrap: line 152 breaks the phrase across `which` / `tests`, the other two do not.

### 1. Is the rewritten sentence true? Yes — all of it.

- **"for some of them"** — correct, and correctly not "every". Of the 7 registered tests that take the binary (`journey`, `journey-tui`, `eof`, `help`, `tui`, `tournament`, `golden`), exactly 3 have the script deciding which tree is read. The other 4 read nothing from any tree: `journey.sh` has no `srcdir`, no `dirname`, no `sst.doc`, and its scripted input (line 70) never issues `help`; `eof.sh` takes only the binary and runs in a `mktemp -d`; `tournament.sh`'s only `$0` uses are awk field references, and its `sst.doc` mentions are all comments citing the manual for hard-coded expectations. - **`help` and `tui` find `sst.doc` from their own path** — both true, by different mechanisms. `tests/help.sh:27` sets `srcdir` from `dirname $0/..`, then `:65-69` copies `$srcdir/sst.doc` into the scratch dir the game runs in. `tests/tui.sh:40` sets `srcdir` the same way and `:322` sets `startdir="$srcdir"`, which `start()` passes as tmux's `-c`; the comment at `:318-321` gives the reason, and the script really does exercise it — `help move` at `:421`, `help` at `:530` and `:581`.

  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).

  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

in the words you would use if you expected to be argued with.

    Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
    useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

11. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review. A changed state includes code, tests,
      documentation, generated files, conflict resolution, or any other
      staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and
      worktree remain unchanged. The `verifier` follows the same
      condition: what makes either pass run again is a changed state. A
      finding answered by argument alone leaves both passes nothing they
      have not already seen, and a round of findings answered by edits
      takes one rerun over the result rather than one per finding.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and
      any required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not
      open draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a
      draft.

12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed
    when these conditions are met.
    Use squash merge for short-lived development branches to keep `main`
    linear, then delete the merged branch.

### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.

Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent cannot
be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run and the
work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the task, and a
report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was supposed to inform.
The entanglement is the reason, so a faster harness would not change it, and
neither would a focused test cheap enough to look worth handing over.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration. One caveat while it
stands: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is
#125, so say so when invoking the pass.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop in the
step it belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot,
asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,
and step 4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not
give it is visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.

What handing it off buys is context and not time, and the two do not track
each other: a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated,
where one that prints twelve hundred lines is. So delegate when the failing
run would bury this context, which is a property of the test and worth
looking up rather than guessing — one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()`
made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes, `tournament.sh`
dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails, `golden.sh` a diff per
changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are below it — a broken `ctest
-R '^tuifmt$'` reports itself, with `--output-on-failure`, in a few dozen
lines, a broken `help` journey in sixty — there is nothing to bury, so keep
it.

When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,
`-DCLOAKING` and the `-DDEBUG` that Debug builds add all decide which
commands and messages the game has at all.

When it is unclear whether a change reaches the player, run the pass. A
`ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass; code that runs while the
game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.

Skipping it is a decision, not an omission. Say that it was skipped and
why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,
the pull request body and the summary of the work. The last three put it
on the record; the first is the one that reaches a reviewer with a
mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue
about, which is why step 8 asks for it as well. An agent writing that
sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong
pass.

An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot
satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work.

- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.
- **Point at the definitions here rather than restating them.**
  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
  the whole reason this file exists.
- **Keep the three names.** The workflow above, the commit history and the
  issue tracker all refer to them by name.
- **Land the definition as its own change,** on its own branch and commit,
  before the work it will review — not beside a feature, which step 10
  forbids and step 3 argues against. It belongs in the repository rather
  than in someone's local configuration for the same reason this file
  does: the next session in that tool then inherits a reviewer instead of
  improvising one, and an improvised reviewer drifts. That commit is also
  the one place self-review cannot be avoided, since step 8 cannot be
  satisfied by the commit that creates the reviewer. Say so in the commit,
  and disclose it as below.
- **Confirm the harness actually loads what you wrote.** A definition in a
  directory the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside it looks
  exactly like a step that was carried out.
- **Self-review is the last resort, not the default.** Taking it means
  saying which mechanism you looked for and why it was not there — or, for
  the commit that creates the reviewer, that it did not yet exist. Say it
  in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary
  alone when there is no pull request. A reviewer who shares the author's
  memory of what was intended is the one thing this section exists to prevent.

### Answering a finding

Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their passes to one standard, in the same words:
fix every actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly. Two ways to
answer, and silence is neither.

**Fixing** is the ordinary one, and most findings deserve it.

**Resolving explicitly** is for the finding you judge wrong, or right
about something this change is not. Say what you think is true instead,
in the words you would use if you expected to be argued with.

Where it goes depends on whether anything else is going to read the
change. A resolution alters no code, so it triggers no rerun: steps 6,
7 and 8 each condition theirs on a change, and step 11 forbids
repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree. So put it to the
next pass that runs anyway — step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts
into `code-review`, and a `verifier` finding you resolve is one
`code-review` should hear about. For a `code-review` finding resolved
without a change there is no next pass, and the record is the whole
of it.

Either way it goes in the pull request body and in the summary of the
work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request, on the same
terms steps 3 and 9 already set. A resolution nobody can find
afterwards is the silence this rule exists to stop.

What does not count: fixing something adjacent and calling the finding
handled, agreeing and then forgetting, or "I disagree" with no reason
under it. Filing an issue does not answer a finding about *this*
change — step 9 is explicit that filing is not resolving — but a
finding about code the change did not touch is answered by filing it
and saying so, which is step 9 working as intended rather than an
exception to it.
